sections.h2: Where does a Schenectady homeowner pay property tax?
sections.html:
City and county taxes are paid to the City of Schenectady Bureau of Receipts, and school taxes go to the school district. The split matters when you sell, because one payoff letter will not show everything.

According to the Bureau of Receipts page, the city bill combines city and county taxes with water and sewer charges and, where it applies, the trash fee. The same page says school taxes have been paid to the school district rather than at City Hall since 2007 and lists the district's number as 518-881-3988.

The Bureau of Receipts works from City Hall, Room 100, 105 Jay Street, and answers at 518-382-5016. The assessment office is a separate counter in the same building, Room 8.

sections.h2: When are Schenectady tax bills issued and due?
sections.html:
Schenectady issues its tax bills on January 1 of each year, and they are payable quarterly in January, April, July and October. That is a different rhythm from Rochester, Albany or most towns, where the bill arrives in summer or autumn.

The city lists three ways to pay:

  • By mail to City of Schenectady, PO Box 947, Schenectady, New York 12301. Send a check with the detached stub, never cash, and tick the receipt box on the coupon if you want a receipt.
  • In person through the drop box on Franklin Street, using your own envelope for the stub and check or money order. Payments left after hours are processed the next business day.
  • Online through the city's electronic bill pay site, which also lets you look up what is owed.

A payment without the stub is accepted if the property address is written on it. For a closing in the coming weeks, ask the Bureau which quarters are still open.

sections.h2: What is the Schenectady assessment calendar?
sections.html:
The yearly assessment cycle runs from a March 1 taxable status date to a July 1 final roll, with Grievance Day on the fourth Tuesday in May. The city's assessment process page sets out the sequence for the roughly 20,400 parcels inside city limits.

Schenectady yearly assessment dates. Source: City of Schenectady assessment process page.
DateWhat happens
March 1Taxable status date, and the last day to file exemption applications for the year
May 1Tentative roll filed and the grievance period opens
Fourth Tuesday in MayGrievance Day before the Board of Assessment Review
July 1Final roll filed

The 2026 grievance period ran from May 1 through 8 p.m. on Tuesday, May 26, 2026, so it is over. The next one opens May 1, 2027, and Grievance Day that year is May 25.

sections.h2: How do I file a grievance on my Schenectady assessment?
sections.html:
Send the state grievance form, RP-524, to the City Assessor by mail, by email at grievance@schenectadyny.gov, or by hand at 105 Jay Street, Room 8. The assessment office phone is 518-382-5075.

Details the city spells out for filers:

  • Email applications should carry the property address and the SBL (tax map) number in the subject line, with the form attached as a PDF.
  • For mailed forms, include a self-addressed stamped envelope or an email address so the office can send back a receipt.
  • Hand-delivered forms get a photocopy of the first page as the receipt.
  • The board reads every application received during the period, even if you never appear in person, and skipping the hearing does not count against you.

The grievance route works only inside the window above, so a seller who is past it should price the house with the current assessment in mind.

sections.h2: What does the Schenectady assessment roll tell a seller?
sections.html:
The roll lists the property class, build year, condition, bedrooms, baths, fireplaces and square footage the assessor has on file, so a seller can check them before a buyer does. A wrong bedroom count or a missing note about a gutted kitchen changes the value the city assigns.

Property class codes on the roll read 210 for a single family house, 220 for two family, 230 for three family and 280 for a multiple residence. Land frontage and depth come from tax maps supplied by Schenectady County Real Property. If something on the card is wrong, call the assessment office at 518-382-5075 and ask how to correct it.

sections.h2: How do I find out which exemptions apply to my Schenectady house?
sections.html:
Call the assessment office at 518-382-5075 and ask for the list of exemptions the city offers. The city says it administers real property tax exemptions for eligible individuals and organizations, and the filing deadline for the current year is the March 1 taxable status date.

The state tax department publishes the downloadable exemption forms, and the city's assessment page links to its guidance on contesting an assessment. A buyer who plans to live in the house will need to file their own applications after closing, so mention the March 1 date to them if the sale falls in winter.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Schenectady taxes?
sections.html:
An unpaid balance stays attached to the parcel, and the Bureau of Receipts is the office to ask for the exact amount and which quarters are open. The city page does not post a penalty schedule, so request the figure by phone or at the counter rather than guessing.

New York sets a two-year redemption period for property under a delinquent tax lien, and a taxing district can lengthen it for homes. That rule is in RPTL section 1110.

Ask for a payoff in writing, and ask the school district for its own figure, since school taxes are collected separately.

sections.h2: How are taxes handled when I sell a house in Schenectady?
sections.html:
The closing agent requests payoff amounts from the Bureau of Receipts and the school district and pays them from the sale price, so owing tax does not stop a sale. It only lowers your net.

The city bill folds in water, sewer and the trash fee, which means an old utility balance can sit inside what looks like a tax figure. Read the breakdown line by line. If a quarter has just come due, ask whether the closing agent will treat it as owed by you or prorate it with the buyer.

Sellers of older houses should also expect questions from buyers. The Wikipedia article on Schenectady describes the General Electric Realty Plot beside Union College as an early planned neighborhood of large homes in Tudor, Dutch Colonial and Queen Anne styles, which gives a sense of how old parts of the housing stock are.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about Schenectady housing?
sections.html:
About 45.6 percent of Schenectady homes are owner-occupied, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate puts the population at 69,471, up 3.6 percent from the April 2020 base. The city covers 10.79 square miles of land, which works out to about 6,213 people per square mile in 2020.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020-2024: $168,800.
  • Median gross rent: $1,145.
  • Households: 29,184, at 2.22 persons each.
  • Median household income: $58,399.
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,596.

Schenectady sits near the meeting of the Mohawk and Hudson rivers, about 15 miles from Albany, and was settled by Dutch colonists in the 1600s. It grew around the Erie Canal corridor and companies such as General Electric and the American Locomotive Company. The Stockade Historic District includes restored Dutch homes.

faqs.q: How many times a year are Schenectady taxes due?
faqs.a: Four. Bills are issued January 1 and payable in January, April, July and October. School tax is a separate payment made to the school district.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Schenectady tax online?
faqs.a: Yes. The city runs an electronic bill pay site, and the Bureau of Receipts also takes mail payments and check or money order drops in the Franklin Street box.
The fourth Tuesday in May. The 2026 date was May 26 and has passed, and the 2027 date falls on May 25, with the grievance period opening May 1.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Schenectady exemption?
faqs.a: Call the assessment office at 518-382-5075 or visit City Hall, Room 8. Exemption applications are due by the March 1 taxable status date.

faqs.q: Does my Schenectady tax bill include school tax?
faqs.a: No. The city bill covers city and county taxes plus water, sewer and the trash fee where it applies, and school tax is paid to the district. Ask both offices for payoff figures before you close.
